position: attributive only — before a noun; only the fixed phrase *reign supreme* comes after a verb

senses.gloss: Highest in rank, power or authority.
examples: The *Supreme* Court agreed to hear the case.
He was the *supreme* commander of the allied forces.
In this house the cat reigns *supreme*.

senses.gloss: Greatest possible in degree.
examples: It took a *supreme* effort to keep from laughing.
She testified with *supreme* confidence.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a sure-fire hit*
contrast: Often written as one word: *surefire*. It is informal, and it stays before the noun.

senses.gloss: Certain to work or to succeed.
examples: Lemon bars are a *sure-fire* crowd-pleaser.
There's no *sure-fire* way to get a toddler to sleep.
Asking about his kids is a *sure-fire* way to start a conversation.

position: both — *a sure-footed mule*, *The mule is sure-footed*

senses.gloss: Able to walk or climb without slipping.
examples: Goats are remarkably *sure-footed* on bare rock.
You want a *sure-footed* horse on this trail.

senses.gloss: Confident and unlikely to make a mistake.
examples: The new mayor has been *sure-footed* in her first month.
It's a *sure-footed* performance from a young actor.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a surface-to-air missile*

senses.gloss: Fired from the ground at something flying.
examples: The base is defended by *surface-to-air* missiles.
They brought the drone down with a *surface-to-air* system.
*Surface-to-air* batteries ring the capital.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *surgical gloves*

senses.gloss: Having to do with surgery.
examples: The nurse handed him a *surgical* mask.
This needs a *surgical* solution, not more pills.

senses.gloss: Done with great precision, hitting only what is aimed at.
examples: The air force called it a *surgical* strike.
She cut the paragraph with *surgical* precision.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *surging prices*

senses.gloss: Rising quickly and by a lot.
examples: *Surging* rents pushed families out of the city.
The company blamed *surging* costs for the layoffs.

senses.gloss: Moving forward in a powerful wave.
examples: The *surging* crowd carried us toward the gate.
*Surging* water tore the dock loose.

position: both — *a surly waiter*, *He got surly*

senses.gloss: Rude and unfriendly in a bad-tempered way.
examples: The waiter was *surly* and slow.
He gave me a *surly* look and went back to his phone.
Teenagers get *surlier* when they're tired.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *surplus cash*
contrast: Also a noun: *a budget surplus*, *the city has a surplus*. The opposite noun is *a deficit*.

senses.gloss: Left over after what is needed has been used.
examples: The store sells *surplus* army gear.
We put the *surplus* money into savings.
*Surplus* grain is sold abroad.

position: both — *a surreal scene*, *The whole thing felt surreal*

senses.gloss: So strange that it feels like a dream and not like real life.
examples: The whole evening felt *surreal*.
It was *surreal* to see my own face on a billboard.
The movie has a *surreal*, dreamlike quality.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a surreptitious glance*

senses.gloss: Done quietly and in secret, so that nobody notices.
examples: She took a *surreptitious* glance at her phone.
He made a *surreptitious* copy of the file.
They exchanged *surreptitious* looks across the table.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a surrogate mother*
contrast: Also a noun: *the surrogate gave birth in March*; in politics a *surrogate* is someone who speaks for a candidate.

senses.gloss: Taking the place of someone or something else.
examples: Her aunt was a *surrogate* mother to her.
The couple is working with a *surrogate* mother.
Test scores are a *surrogate* measure of what kids actually learned.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *the surrounding hills*
contrast: The plural noun *surroundings* means окружение, обстановка: *The cat is nervous in new surroundings*.

senses.gloss: Lying all around a place.
examples: The fire spread to the *surrounding* woods.
People came from Dallas and the *surrounding* towns.
You can see the *surrounding* countryside from the tower.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *the surviving crew*

senses.gloss: Still alive after others have died.
examples: He is the last *surviving* member of the band.
The *surviving* passengers were flown home.

senses.gloss: Still in existence after a long time.
examples: It's the only *surviving* copy of the letter.
The *surviving* sections of the wall date from 1780.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *He is susceptible to flattery*

senses.gloss: Easily affected or harmed by something.
examples: Older people are more *susceptible* to the flu.
These plants are *susceptible* to frost.

senses.gloss: Easily influenced by other people or by feelings.
examples: He's *susceptible* to flattery.
Young fans are *susceptible* to this kind of advertising.

position: both — *a suspect package*, *His motives are suspect*
contrast: Stress separates the words: the adjective and the noun are SUS-pekt (*suspect data*, *the suspect fled*), the verb is suh-SPEKT (*I suspect he knows*).

senses.gloss: Probably dishonest, unreliable or dangerous.
examples: His motives are *suspect*.
Police blew up a *suspect* package at the station.
The numbers in that report look *suspect* to me.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a suspected leak*; after a verb it is the passive verb, not the adjective
contrast: *Suspected* is what people believe is true (*a suspected case of measles*); *suspicious* is what looks wrong (*suspicious behavior*).

senses.gloss: Believed, but not proved, to be the thing named.
examples: Doctors reported two *suspected* cases of measles.
The *suspected* cause is a gas leak.
Police arrested the *suspected* driver an hour later.

position: both — *a suspended ceiling*, *Her license is suspended*

senses.gloss: Hanging from something above.
examples: A microphone was *suspended* over the stage.
The kitchen has *suspended* lights over the island.

senses.gloss: Officially stopped for a period of time.
examples: He got a *suspended* sentence and no jail time.
Her license is *suspended* until March.

position: both — *a suspenseful movie*, *The ending is suspenseful*

senses.gloss: Keeping you tense and eager to know what happens next.
examples: The last twenty minutes are really *suspenseful*.
She writes *suspenseful* thrillers set in small towns.
It's a quiet book, but the ending is *suspenseful*.

position: both — *suspicious behavior*, *She was suspicious*
takes: *of* + noun or *-ing* (who or what you suspect); *that*-clause
contrast: It works both ways: *He is suspicious* can mean he suspects someone, or that he looks like a criminal — the *of*-phrase settles it. *Suspicious* is how something looks; *suspected* is what people believe.

senses.gloss: Feeling that something is wrong or that someone is lying.
examples: She was *suspicious* of his sudden generosity.
I'm *suspicious* that they knew all along.

senses.gloss: Making people think that something is wrong.
examples: Neighbors reported a *suspicious* van on the street.
There was nothing *suspicious* about the fire.

position: both — *sustainable farming*, *The pace isn't sustainable*

senses.gloss: Using resources in a way that does not use them up or damage the planet.
examples: The farm uses *sustainable* methods.
Bamboo is a more *sustainable* material than plastic.

senses.gloss: Able to be kept going at the same level.
examples: That pace isn't *sustainable* over a whole season.
They want growth that is *sustainable* without more debt.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *sustained applause*

senses.gloss: Continuing at the same level for a long time.
examples: The speech got a full minute of *sustained* applause.
It will take a *sustained* effort to fix the schools.
The region has seen *sustained* growth for a decade.

position: both — *a svelte dancer*, *She looked svelte*
contrast: A complimentary word, used of people and of sleek objects; *skinny* and *scrawny* are the unkind ones.

senses.gloss: Slim and elegant.
examples: She looked *svelte* in a plain black dress.
The new laptop is *svelte* enough to disappear in a bag.
He came back from the trip tanned and *svelte*.

position: both — *swampy ground*, *The yard is swampy*

senses.gloss: Soft, wet and muddy like a swamp.
examples: The back half of the yard is *swampy* after a storm.
They built the road across *swampy* ground.
The trail gets *swampier* the closer you get to the lake.

position: both — *a swanky hotel*, *The place is swanky*
contrast: Informal and a little teasing — it hints that the money is on display. *Elegant* is the straight compliment.

senses.gloss: Expensive and stylish in a showy way.
examples: They had dinner at a *swanky* hotel downtown.
It's a *swanky* neighborhood — nothing sells under a million.
His new office is *swankier* than mine.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *a swarthy sailor*
contrast: Mostly met in older fiction, and often stereotyping when used of people today; *dark-skinned* or *olive-skinned* is the neutral choice.

senses.gloss: Having dark skin.
examples: The captain was a *swarthy* man with a gold tooth.
In the novel every villain is *swarthy* and foreign.
He was *swarthier* than his brothers.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a swashbuckling pirate*

senses.gloss: Full of bold, romantic adventure, like an old pirate story.
examples: It's an old-fashioned *swashbuckling* adventure movie.
He plays a *swashbuckling* pirate captain.
She wrote *swashbuckling* tales of the high seas.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *sweeping changes*

senses.gloss: Affecting a great many things; wide in scope.
examples: The new law makes *sweeping* changes to the tax code.
The changes are more *sweeping* than anyone expected.

senses.gloss: Too general — made without looking at the details.
examples: That's a *sweeping* generalization about an entire country.
He made *sweeping* claims he couldn't back up.

senses.gloss: Wide and curving, of a view or a line.
examples: The house has a *sweeping* view of the bay.
A *sweeping* staircase curves up from the lobby.

position: both — *a sweet apple*, *The tea is too sweet*
takes: *of* + person in *That's sweet of you*; *on* + person, informal (*He's sweet on her*)
contrast: *Sweet* is the taste itself; *sweetened* means sugar was added. As a noun, *sweets* is candy; British English uses *a sweet* for dessert, American English says *dessert*.

senses.gloss: Tasting of sugar.
examples: The corn was *sweet* and fresh.
This lemonade is too *sweet* for me.
Georgia peaches are *sweeter* than the ones at the store.

senses.gloss: Kind, gentle and lovable.
examples: What a *sweet* little kid.
It was *sweet* of you to call.

senses.gloss: Pleasant to smell, to hear or to experience.
examples: The *sweet* smell of cut grass came through the window.
After that season, the win was especially *sweet*.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *sweet-smelling flowers*

senses.gloss: Having a pleasant smell.
examples: The room was full of *sweet-smelling* flowers.
She uses a *sweet-smelling* soap from the farmers market.
*Sweet-smelling* smoke drifted over from the grill.

position: both — *sweetened tea*, *The yogurt is already sweetened*
contrast: *Sweetened* means sugar or syrup was added; *sweet* is just the taste. The canned milk is *sweetened condensed milk*, never *sweet condensed milk*.

senses.gloss: Made sweet by adding sugar or another sweetener.
examples: He drinks *sweetened* iced tea by the gallon.
The recipe calls for *sweetened* condensed milk.
This yogurt is lightly *sweetened* with honey.

position: both — *a swell idea*, *That's swell*
contrast: Dated and informal: you meet it in old movies and in dry sarcasm (*Oh, that's just swell*). *Swell* is also a verb (*My ankle swelled up*) and a noun (*a big swell out past the reef*).

senses.gloss: Very good — an old-fashioned way of saying great.
examples: That's a *swell* idea.
We had a *swell* time at the lake.
Oh, *swell* — now the printer is broken.

position: both — *a sweltering afternoon*, *It was sweltering*

senses.gloss: Uncomfortably hot and humid.
examples: It was *sweltering* in the car.
They practiced through a *sweltering* August afternoon.
The kitchen gets *sweltering* when the oven is on.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *a swift reply*
contrast: *Swift* is more formal than *fast* and goes with actions and reactions more than with machines: *a swift response*, but *a fast car*. A *swift* is also a small bird.

senses.gloss: Happening or done very quickly.
examples: The response from the city was *swift*.
He gave a *swift* nod and walked out.

senses.gloss: Moving fast.
examples: The river is *swifter* here than it is downstream.
A *swift* current pulled the boat sideways.

position: both — *a swollen ankle*, *My hand is swollen*

senses.gloss: Bigger than normal because of injury or illness.
examples: Her ankle was *swollen* and purple.
He woke up with *swollen* glands.

senses.gloss: Filled past its usual size, especially with water.
examples: The creek was *swollen* with snowmelt.
*Swollen* rivers flooded the low fields.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *sworn testimony*, *sworn enemies*

senses.gloss: Given or made under oath.
examples: The lawyer read his *sworn* statement aloud.
Only *sworn* officers can make the arrest.

senses.gloss: Declared once and for good — of enemies and promises.
examples: The two families have been *sworn* enemies for years.
He is a *sworn* opponent of the whole program.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *sycophantic praise*
contrast: A false friend: Russian *сикофант* is a slanderer or informer, while English *sycophant* is a подхалим — someone who flatters a powerful person.

senses.gloss: Praising a powerful person in an insincere way to get something.
examples: The interview was *sycophantic* from the first question.
He's surrounded by *sycophantic* aides who agree with everything.
Her review of the album is embarrassingly *sycophantic*.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *a symbiotic relationship*

senses.gloss: Describing two living things that live together and help each other.
examples: Clownfish and anemones have a *symbiotic* relationship.
The fungus forms a *symbiotic* bond with the tree roots.

senses.gloss: Describing two people or groups who each need the other.
examples: Reporters and campaigns have a *symbiotic* relationship.
The two companies grew in a *symbiotic* way.

position: both — *a symbolic gesture*, *The dove is symbolic of peace*

senses.gloss: Standing for something else.
examples: The dove is *symbolic* of peace.
Every color in the painting is *symbolic*.

senses.gloss: Done to make a point rather than to have a real effect.
examples: The fine was *symbolic* — twenty dollars.
It was a *symbolic* vote with no legal force.

position: both — *a symmetrical design*, *The garden is symmetrical*
contrast: Also written *symmetric*, mostly in math and science: *a symmetric matrix*.

senses.gloss: Having two halves that match exactly.
examples: The garden is perfectly *symmetrical*.
Her face is more *symmetrical* than most.
Draw a *symmetrical* pattern on both sides of the fold.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *symphonic music*
contrast: The orchestra itself is a *symphony orchestra*, with the noun: *symphonic orchestra* sounds wrong to Americans.

senses.gloss: Of or like a symphony and the large orchestra that plays one.
examples: He writes *symphonic* music for films.
The band's new album has a *symphonic* sound.
A *symphonic* poem tells a story without words.

position: both — mostly after a verb, with *of*

senses.gloss: Being a sign of a larger problem.
examples: The delays are *symptomatic* of a bigger management problem.
Empty storefronts are *symptomatic* of the whole town's decline.

senses.gloss: Showing the symptoms of a disease.
examples: Only *symptomatic* patients were tested at first.
She tested positive but never became *symptomatic*.

position: both — *synchronized swimming*, *The clocks are synchronized*
contrast: American spelling is *-ized*; *synchronised* is British. The Olympic sport is officially *artistic swimming* now, but people still say *synchronized swimming*.

senses.gloss: Made to happen at the same time or at the same speed.
examples: The audio and the video aren't *synchronized*.
She swam on a *synchronized* swimming team in college.
All the traffic lights on Main are *synchronized*.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *a syncopated beat*

senses.gloss: Having the musical accent on the off beats instead of the strong ones.
examples: The song has a *syncopated* beat you can't sit still to.
Ragtime is built on *syncopated* rhythms.
The drums stay *syncopated* through the whole verse.

position: both — almost always after a verb, with *with*

senses.gloss: Having the same meaning as another word.
examples: *Big* and *large* are nearly *synonymous*.
The two terms are *synonymous* in everyday speech.

senses.gloss: So closely connected that one makes you think of the other.
examples: His name became *synonymous* with the city itself.
For my grandparents, Detroit was *synonymous* with cars.

position: both — *a synthetic fabric*, *The fibers are synthetic*
comparison: not gradable — but *more synthetic* is possible about a sound or a feeling

senses.gloss: Made by a chemical process instead of coming from nature.
examples: The jacket is filled with a *synthetic* material.
*Synthetic* rubber holds up better in the cold.
Most of the vitamins on that shelf are *synthetic*.

senses.gloss: Not genuine — made to look or sound real.
examples: The dialogue felt *synthetic*.
There was something *synthetic* about his enthusiasm.

position: both — *Syrian food*, *Her husband is Syrian*
contrast: Always capitalized, and the same word names the people: *a Syrian family*, *He's Syrian*, *two Syrians*.

senses.gloss: Of or from Syria, its people or its culture.
examples: We ate at a *Syrian* restaurant on Fifth Street.
She studies *Syrian* history.
My co-worker is *Syrian*.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *a systematic search*
contrast: *Systematic* means done step by step, on a plan; *systemic* means built into the whole system: *a systematic search* but *systemic corruption*.

senses.gloss: Done carefully, in an organized, step-by-step way.
examples: They made a *systematic* search of the building.
We need a more *systematic* way to track orders.
The report describes *systematic* abuse over many years.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *systemic failure*
contrast: Don't mix it up with *systematic*, which means methodical. *Systemic* means running through the whole system: *systemic racism*, *a systemic infection*.

senses.gloss: Affecting a whole organization or society, not just one part of it.
examples: The audit found *systemic* problems, not one bad manager.
They call it a *systemic* failure of oversight.

senses.gloss: Affecting the entire body, in medicine.
examples: The infection became *systemic*.
*Systemic* drugs travel through the bloodstream.

position: both — *a taboo subject*, *Money talk is taboo here*
contrast: Also a noun: *breaking a taboo*. The stress is on the second syllable: tuh-BOO.

senses.gloss: Not allowed to be talked about or done, by custom.
examples: Money is still a *taboo* subject in many families.
In his house, politics at dinner was *taboo*.
The play deals with *taboo* topics.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *tacit approval*
contrast: *Tacit* means understood without being said. It has nothing to do with *tact* — that word gives *tactful* and *tactless*.

senses.gloss: Understood or agreed to without being said out loud.
examples: The plan had the boss's *tacit* approval.
There was a *tacit* understanding that nobody would mention it.
Silence here counts as *tacit* consent.

position: both — *a taciturn man*, *He gets taciturn*

senses.gloss: Saying very little by nature.
examples: Her father was a *taciturn* man who answered in one word.
He gets *taciturn* when he's working something out.
The two *taciturn* brothers ran the farm together.

position: both — *a tacky souvenir*, *The paint is still tacky*

senses.gloss: Cheap-looking and in poor taste.
examples: The lobby is full of *tacky* gold furniture.
It felt *tacky* to bring up money at the funeral.
Every year their holiday sweaters get *tackier*.

senses.gloss: Slightly sticky, like paint that isn't dry yet.
examples: The varnish is still *tacky*.
The floor felt *tacky* under our shoes.

position: both — *a tactful answer*, *She was tactful about it*

senses.gloss: Careful not to say the thing that would hurt or embarrass someone.
examples: She found a *tactful* way to say no.
He's honest but never *tactful*.
It wasn't *tactful* to bring up his ex.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *a tactical error*
contrast: *Tactical* is about the short-term moves; *strategic* is about the long-term plan: *a tactical retreat* serves *a strategic goal*.

senses.gloss: Having to do with the moves you make to reach a goal.
examples: Pulling out of the deal was a *tactical* mistake.
The coach made a *tactical* decision to rest him.

senses.gloss: Used on the battlefield, at short range — of weapons and units.
examples: The unit trains for *tactical* operations in cities.
*Tactical* nuclear weapons have a short range.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *tactile feedback*
contrast: Also said TAK-tyl. American *-ile* words vary: *fragile* is FRAJ-uhl, *mobile* is MOH-buhl.

senses.gloss: Having to do with the sense of touch.
examples: Babies learn through *tactile* exploration.
A glass screen gives you no *tactile* feedback.

senses.gloss: Pleasant or interesting to touch.
examples: The book has a lovely *tactile* cover.
She likes *tactile* fabrics like velvet and raw wool.

position: both — *a tactless remark*, *That was tactless*

senses.gloss: Saying the wrong thing without thinking how it will land.
examples: That was a *tactless* thing to say to a new widow.
He isn't cruel, just *tactless*.
Her *tactless* question silenced the table.

position: both — *Tahitian pearls*, *Her mother is Tahitian*

senses.gloss: Of or from Tahiti, its people or its language.
examples: We stayed in a *Tahitian* village for a week.
She collects *Tahitian* pearls.
The hotel serves a *Tahitian* breakfast of fruit and coconut.

position: both — *a tailor-made suit*, *The job is tailor-made for her*

senses.gloss: Made to fit one particular person, of clothes.
examples: He wore a *tailor-made* suit to the hearing.
Her winter coat is *tailor-made*.

senses.gloss: Perfectly suited to a person or a purpose.
examples: The job is *tailor-made* for her.
It was a *tailor-made* excuse to leave early.

position: both — *a tailored jacket*, *The course is tailored to beginners*

senses.gloss: Cut to fit closely and neatly, of clothes.
examples: She wore a *tailored* gray jacket.
The pants are *tailored* and a little too tight.

senses.gloss: Made or changed to fit a particular need.
examples: The lessons are *tailored* to each student.
We offer plans *tailored* to small businesses.

position: both — *tainted meat*, *The evidence was tainted*

senses.gloss: Spoiled or made unsafe by something harmful in it.
examples: Dozens of people got sick from *tainted* lettuce.
The well water was *tainted* with gasoline.

senses.gloss: Damaged in its reputation or fairness.
examples: The verdict was *tainted* by the leaked photos.
He left office with a *tainted* record.

position: both — *Taiwanese food*, *The company is Taiwanese*
contrast: Like all *-ese* words it adds no *-s* for people: *three Taiwanese engineers*. For one person say *a Taiwanese woman*, not *a Taiwanese*.

senses.gloss: Of or from Taiwan, its people or its culture.
examples: We had *Taiwanese* beef noodle soup.
The chip company is *Taiwanese*.
*Taiwanese* students make up a big part of the program.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *take-home pay*

senses.gloss: Left over after taxes are taken out, of pay.
examples: My *take-home* pay is about two-thirds of that number.
The raise barely changed her *take-home* amount.

senses.gloss: Meant to be taken away and used or done at home.
examples: The final is a *take-home* exam.
The *take-home* message is simple: start early.

position: predicative only — after a verb: *That seat is taken*
comparison: not gradable — but *very taken with* is common
contrast: Of a person, *He's taken* means he is already in a relationship.

senses.gloss: Already used, occupied or claimed.
examples: Sorry, this seat is *taken*.
Every decent username was already *taken*.

senses.gloss: Charmed or impressed by someone or something.
examples: She was quite *taken* with the little house.
I'm not *taken* with the new design.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *takeout food*
contrast: Also a noun: *Let's get takeout tonight*. The British say *takeaway*. Written as one word for the adjective, two for the verb: *take out the trash*.

senses.gloss: Sold to be carried away and eaten somewhere else.
examples: The fridge is full of *takeout* containers.
We ordered *takeout* pizza and watched a movie.
The place has a *takeout* window on the side.

position: both — *a talented singer*, *The cast is talented*

senses.gloss: Having a natural ability to do something well.
examples: She's a *talented* cellist.
He's the most *talented* kid in the program.
The cast is young and *talented*.

position: both — *a talentless hack*, *The band is talentless*

senses.gloss: Having no skill or ability at all.
examples: The critics called the band *talentless*.
He isn't *talentless* — he just never practices.
It's a *talentless* remake of a good movie.

position: both — *a talkative kid*, *He gets talkative*
contrast: *Talkative* is neutral, *chatty* is warm, *long-winded* is the unkind one.

senses.gloss: Talking a lot, or liking to talk.
examples: He gets *talkative* after one beer.
She's a *talkative* kid who narrates everything she does.
The driver wasn't *talkative*, which was fine with me.

position: both — *a tall building*, *He's tall*
contrast: *Tall* is for people, trees, buildings and other narrow things; mountains and flying planes are *high*. With a measurement the adjective comes last: *six feet tall*, never *tall six feet*.

senses.gloss: Of more than average height.
examples: Her brother is very *tall*.
They planted *tall* grass along the fence.
He's the *tallest* player on the team.

senses.gloss: Hard to believe or hard to do — in fixed phrases.
examples: Getting there by six is a *tall* order.
Grandpa told us another *tall* tale about the war.

position: both — *a tame rabbit*, *The movie is pretty tame*
contrast: *Tame* is also a verb: *They tamed the horse in a week*.

senses.gloss: Not wild — used to people and not dangerous.
examples: The deer in the park are almost *tame*.
She kept a *tame* crow that rode on her shoulder.

senses.gloss: Milder or duller than you expected.
examples: The movie is pretty *tame* for an R rating.
The party was *tamer* than last year.

position: both — *a Tamil family*, *Her husband is Tamil*
contrast: Always capitalized, and the same word names the people and the language: *Tamil food*, *She speaks Tamil*.

senses.gloss: Of the Tamil people of southern India and Sri Lanka, or their language.
examples: He grew up in a *Tamil* neighborhood in Chennai.
The restaurant serves *Tamil* food.
*Tamil* movies are big business.

position: both — *tan pants*, *She's really tan*
contrast: Double the *n*: *tanner*, *tannest*. *Tan* is also a verb (*I burn, I don't tan*) and a noun (*She came back with a great tan*).

senses.gloss: Of a light yellowish-brown color.
examples: He wore *tan* khakis and a blue shirt.
They picked a *tan* carpet for the hallway.

senses.gloss: Having skin darkened by the sun.
examples: She came back from Florida *tan* and rested.
He's *tanner* now than he was in May.

position: both — mostly after a verb, with *to*

senses.gloss: Only slightly connected to the main subject.
examples: That point is *tangential* to what we're discussing.
He kept going off on *tangential* stories about his cousin.
Her role in the project was *tangential* at best.

position: both — *tangible results*, *The benefit is tangible*

senses.gloss: Real and clear enough to be seen, measured or pointed to.
examples: We need *tangible* results by June.
There's no *tangible* evidence of a leak.

senses.gloss: Able to be touched.
examples: The tension in the room was almost *tangible*.
Cash in your hand is *tangible* in a way a number on a screen isn't.

position: both — *tangled hair*, *The cords got tangled*

senses.gloss: Twisted together into a knot or a mess.
examples: Her hair was *tangled* from the wind.
The headphones came out of my bag *tangled* again.

senses.gloss: Confusingly complicated.
examples: It's a *tangled* story with too many people in it.
The company sits behind a *tangled* web of subsidiaries.

position: both — *a tangy sauce*, *The dressing is tangy*

senses.gloss: Having a strong, pleasantly sharp or sour taste or smell.
examples: The sauce is sweet and *tangy*.
I like a *tangy* goat cheese on that salad.
This lemonade is *tangier* than the last batch.

position: both — *tanned arms*, *He came back tanned*
contrast: *Tanned* and *tan* both describe sun-darkened skin, and Americans often just say *tan*: *She's very tan*. Leather is *tanned* too — that is the older meaning.

senses.gloss: Having skin made browner by the sun.
examples: He came back from Greece *tanned* and relaxed.
Her *tanned* arms stood out against the white shirt.
Everyone on the boat was *tanned* by the second day.

position: both — *a tantalizing hint*, *The smell was tantalizing*
contrast: American spelling is *-izing*; *tantalising* is British.

senses.gloss: Attractive in a way that makes you want something you can't quite have.
examples: The smell from the kitchen was *tantalizing*.
She dropped a *tantalizing* hint about the ending.
The offer was *tantalizing*, but the timing was wrong.

position: predicative only — after a verb, always with *to*

senses.gloss: Equal in effect to something bad, even if it isn't called that.
examples: Saying nothing here is *tantamount* to agreeing.
The memo was *tantamount* to an admission of guilt.
Refusing the test is *tantamount* to a confession.

position: both — *the Tanzanian coast*, *Our guide is Tanzanian*

senses.gloss: Of or from Tanzania or its people.
examples: The *Tanzanian* coast is beautiful in February.
Our guide was *Tanzanian*.
She works with a *Tanzanian* coffee cooperative.

position: both — *a Taoist temple*, *His teacher is Taoist*
contrast: Usually said with a *d*: DOW-ist, rhyming with *now*; TOW-ist is also heard. The newer spelling is *Daoist*, and the same word names a follower.

senses.gloss: Of Taoism, the Chinese philosophy and religion, or its followers.
examples: We visited a *Taoist* temple outside the city.
He studies *Taoist* philosophy.
The book explains *Taoist* ideas about nature.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *tapered jeans*

senses.gloss: Getting narrower toward one end.
examples: He wears *tapered* jeans now.
The candle has a *tapered* top.
The legs of the table are gently *tapered*.

position: both — *a tardy student*, *He was tardy again*
contrast: In American schools it is the official word for late, and it is even a noun there: *three tardies and you get detention*.

senses.gloss: Arriving later than you should.
examples: He was *tardy* twice this week.
*Tardy* students have to check in at the office.

senses.gloss: Coming later than it should have.
examples: The city's response was *tardy* and half-hearted.
Her thank-you notes get *tardier* every year.

position: both — *a tart apple*, *These cherries are tart*
contrast: *Tart* is also a noun — a small open fruit pie.

senses.gloss: Pleasantly sour in taste.
examples: These cherries are *tart*.
A *tart* apple works better in a pie.
The green ones are *tarter* than the red.

senses.gloss: Sharp and a little unkind, of a remark or a tone.
examples: She gave a *tart* reply and hung up.
His reviews are famous for their *tart* humor.

position: both — *the Tasmanian coast*, *Her mother is Tasmanian*
contrast: The *Tasmanian devil* is a real animal about the size of a small dog, not only a cartoon.

senses.gloss: Of or from Tasmania, the island state of Australia.
examples: The *Tasmanian* devil hunts at night.
We hiked along the *Tasmanian* coast.
Her mother is *Tasmanian*.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *tasseled loafers*
contrast: American spelling keeps one *l*: *tasseled*; British doubles it, *tasselled*.

senses.gloss: Decorated with tassels.
examples: He wore *tasseled* loafers with no socks.
A *tasseled* lamp shade sat on the piano.
The graduates threw their *tasseled* caps in the air.

position: both — *a tasteful room*, *The tribute was tasteful*
contrast: *Tasteful* is about good taste in style, never about flavor — food that tastes good is *tasty*.

senses.gloss: Showing good judgment about style or about what is appropriate.
examples: The apartment is small but *tasteful*.
They sent a *tasteful* arrangement of white flowers.
He made a *tasteful* joke about it, which is harder than it sounds.

position: both — *a tasteless joke*, *The soup was tasteless*

senses.gloss: Offensive or in bad taste.
examples: He told a *tasteless* joke about the accident.
The ad was widely called *tasteless*.

senses.gloss: Having no flavor at all.
examples: The soup was warm and *tasteless*.
Hospital food is famously *tasteless*.

position: both — *a tasty sandwich*, *That was tasty*
contrast: *Tasty* is about flavor; *tasteful* is about style. For Russian *вкусный* Americans most often just say *really good*: *This soup is really good*.

senses.gloss: Having a good flavor.
examples: That was a *tasty* sandwich.
She makes a *tasty* black bean soup.
The second batch was *tastier* than the first.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *a tattered flag*

senses.gloss: Old and torn.
examples: He carried a *tattered* paperback everywhere.
The flag over the post office is *tattered*.

senses.gloss: Badly damaged — of a reputation or a relationship.
examples: The deal left his reputation *tattered*.
They're trying to repair a *tattered* friendship.

position: both — *a taupe rug*, *The walls are taupe*
contrast: One syllable, like *tope*: TOHP. It names the gray-brown between beige and gray, and it is also a noun: *a soft taupe*.

senses.gloss: Of a grayish-brown color.
examples: The walls in the hallway are *taupe*.
She picked a *taupe* rug for the bedroom.
*Taupe* curtains warm up a gray room.

position: both — *a taut rope*, *Pull the line taut*
contrast: *Taut* sounds exactly like *taught*, the past of *teach*: keep the rope *taut*; the class was *taught* by a substitute.

senses.gloss: Stretched tight.
examples: Pull the line *taut* and tie it off.
The tent ropes were *taut* in the wind.
Get the wire *tauter* or the fence will sag.

senses.gloss: Tense and tightly controlled — of a face, a mood or a story.
examples: His face was *taut* with worry.
It's a *taut* ninety-minute thriller.

position: both — *a tautological definition*, *The argument is tautological*

senses.gloss: Saying the same thing twice in different words, so that it adds nothing.
examples: 'Free gift' is *tautological* — a gift is already free.
His definition is *tautological*: it uses the word it defines.
The whole argument turns out to be *tautological*.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *tawdry souvenirs*

senses.gloss: Cheap and showy.
examples: The casino is all *tawdry* gold and neon.
The shop sells *tawdry* souvenirs to tourists.

senses.gloss: Sordid — morally ugly and a little shabby.
examples: The paper printed every *tawdry* detail.
The story got *tawdrier* with every new witness.

position: both — *a tawny lion*, *The hills turn tawny*

senses.gloss: Of a warm brownish-orange color, like a lion's coat.
examples: A *tawny* lion lay in the shade.
The hills turn *tawny* by August.
Her hair looked *tawnier* in the summer light.

position: both — *a tax-exempt charity*, *The foundation is tax-exempt*
contrast: *Tax-exempt* describes the organization or income that the law excuses from tax; *tax-free* describes money or goods you pay no tax on: *a tax-exempt charity*, *tax-free shopping*.

senses.gloss: Not required to pay tax, or not taxed.
examples: The foundation is *tax-exempt*.
Interest on those bonds is *tax-exempt*.
Churches hold *tax-exempt* status.

position: both — *a tax-free weekend*, *The withdrawal is tax-free*
contrast: In compounds *-free* means without, not at no cost: *tax-free* is без налога, not бесплатный. It is also an adverb: *You can take the money out tax-free*.

senses.gloss: With no tax to pay on it.
examples: The state has a *tax-free* weekend in August.
Withdrawals after age 59 are *tax-free*.
They advertise *tax-free* shopping for tourists.

position: both — *taxable income*, *The prize is taxable*

senses.gloss: That tax must be paid on.
examples: Your *taxable* income is what's left after deductions.
Tips are *taxable*.
The prize money is fully *taxable*.

position: both — *a taxing schedule*, *The trip was taxing*
form: -ing from *tax*, in its older sense of to strain
contrast: Nothing to do with taxes: *a taxing week* is a hard, tiring one.

senses.gloss: Demanding a lot of effort or energy.
examples: It was a *taxing* week for everyone.
The hike isn't *taxing*, just long.
She has a *taxing* job and two small kids.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *taxpaying citizens*
contrast: Also written *tax-paying*. The person is a *taxpayer*, one word.

senses.gloss: Paying taxes.
examples: He says he speaks for ordinary *taxpaying* citizens.
*Taxpaying* businesses want a say in the plan.
They're hard-working, *taxpaying* people.

position: both — *a teachable player*, *The kid is teachable*

senses.gloss: Willing and able to learn.
examples: He's raw but *teachable*.
Coaches look for *teachable* players.

senses.gloss: Able to be taught — of a skill, or of a moment that teaches something.
examples: Empathy is *teachable*, up to a point.
She turned the argument into a *teachable* moment.
